 Let ABC15 Know: Medicare and health insurance scams ramp up during open enrollment: What to watch for
 Health care and Medicare open enrollment are underway, but scammers are also using the season as an opportunity to target consumers. 
 Prev 
 Next 
 By: 
 Christel Bell 
 Posted 
 Share Copy link Facebook Nextdoor X Threads Reddit LinkedIn Email WhatsApp Messenger Print 
 Add ABC15 as a Google Preferred Source 
 PHOENIX, AZ — Fraudsters may pose as government agencies, Medicare representatives or insurance providers. Some offer free health screenings, gifts, lower premiums or special enrollment deals in an attempt to get consumers to provide personal or financial information.
 The Federal Communications Commission warns that scammers are using tactics including spoofed caller ID, phony government-approved plans, QR codes and links that lead to fraudulent enrollment pages, and Medicare voice-phishing schemes that may use AI-generated voices. [fcc.gov] 
 A Medicare-related call shows how the conversation can start
 I recently received an unsolicited call asking whether I was enrolled in Medicare Parts A and B.
 The caller never identified a company or organization but repeatedly asked about my Medicare coverage.
 That's an important reason to be cautious about answering questions or providing information during an unexpected call.
 Dana Marie Kennedy, State Director, with AARP Arizona says consumers should be suspicious of unsolicited contacts involving Medicare.
 "It's important that you know two things: unsolicited contact about Medicare is highly suspicious, and Medicare will never contact you out of the blue," Kennedy said.
 Federal guidance similarly warns consumers about unexpected calls seeking Medicare or other sensitive information. The FCC advises consumers not to provide Social Security numbers, Medicare ID numbers, passwords, account numbers or other sensitive information during an unexpected call or text. [fcc.gov] 
 Warning signs of a Medicare scam
 Consumers should watch for several potential red flags during open enrollment:
 Someone promising free items or services.
 Pressure to switch Medicare plans.
 Claims that you need to renew or upgrade your Medicare card.
 Threats that your coverage will be canceled.
 Claims that you are unexpectedly eligible for a refund.
 Requests for personal information during an unsolicited call or text.
 The FCC identifies these tactics as warning signs consumers should recognize during open enrollment. [fcc.gov] 
 "If you get threats from somebody saying they're going to cancel your coverage, that should also be a red flag," Kennedy said.
 How to protect yourself
 Never give out personal information during an unexpected call or text. Keep your Medicare number, Social Security number and other sensitive information protected.
 Be cautious of anyone offering free gifts or incentives in exchange for information.
 Consumers can also avoid answering calls from numbers they don't recognize. Caller ID isn't always reliable because scammers can spoof a phone number to make a call appear legitimate or familiar. [fcc.gov] 
 If someone contacts you claiming to represent an insurance company or government agency, don't rely on a callback number provided by the caller or in a suspicious message. Instead, independently find the organization's official contact information.
 Where to get trusted enrollment help
 For Medicare information, start with Medicare.gov. Consumers looking for coverage through the Health Insurance Marketplace can use HealthCare.gov. The Health Insurance Marketplace also recommends using official government websites and warns consumers not to provide personal or financial information to someone threatening them or demanding payment to obtain or keep coverage. [healthcare.gov] , [healthcare.gov] 
 Arizonans can also seek assistance through the state's health insurance assistance resources. The Arizona Senior Medicare Patrol provides Medicare fraud prevention information and assistance for Medicare beneficiaries, families and caregivers. [azsmp.org] 
 Arizonans can also find resources at the Area Agency on Aging. 
 The biggest takeaway: Don't let an unexpected call pressure you into making an immediate decision. Hang up, verify who you're dealing with and seek information from a source you trust.
